title: College Algebra and Precalculus
subject: Mathematics

cards.prompt: What is Real Numbers? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: The real numbers consist of rational and irrational numbers and form the usual continuous number line. Every real number has a unique location on that line.
required_concepts: Represent points on the number line.
accepted_variants: The ordered number system represented by the full number line.
major_error_concepts: Claiming every real number is a ratio of integers.

cards.prompt: What is Rational Numbers? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A rational number can be written as p/q for integers p and q with q nonzero. Its decimal expansion terminates or eventually repeats.
major_error_concepts: Calling every nonterminating decimal irrational.

cards.prompt: What is Irrational Numbers? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: An irrational number is a real number that cannot be expressed as a ratio of integers. Its decimal expansion neither terminates nor eventually repeats.
accepted_variants: A real number outside the integer-ratio class.
major_error_concepts: Classifying a repeating decimal as irrational.

cards.prompt: What is Interval Notation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Interval notation describes connected ranges on the real line. Brackets include finite endpoints, parentheses exclude them, and infinite endpoints always use parentheses.
required_concepts: Bracket means included endpoint; parenthesis means excluded.
Infinity is not an included endpoint.
accepted_variants: A compact notation for a real-number range.
major_error_concepts: Writing a closed bracket at positive infinity.

cards.prompt: What is Absolute Value? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: The absolute value |x| is the distance of x from zero. It equals x when x is nonnegative and -x when x is negative, so it is always nonnegative.
accepted_variants: The nonnegative magnitude of a real number.
major_error_concepts: Assuming |x| = x when x is negative.

cards.prompt: What is Order Properties? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Order properties govern inequalities on the real line. Adding the same number preserves an inequality, multiplying by a positive number preserves it, and multiplying by a negative number reverses it.
required_concepts: Negative multiplication reverses the inequality direction.
accepted_variants: Rules for preserving or reversing comparisons.
major_error_concepts: Multiplying both sides by a negative number without reversing the comparison.

cards.prompt: State the main exponent laws and a sufficient real-domain condition under which all three hold.
cards.definition: For a positive real base a and real exponents m,n, a^m a^n=a^(m+n), a^m/a^n=a^(m-n), and (a^m)^n=a^(mn). For integer exponents these identities also apply to nonzero real bases. Do not extend the power-of-a-power rule to negative bases with arbitrary fractional exponents; real-defined expressions alone do not guarantee it.
required_concepts: State the product, quotient, and power-of-a-power identities.
Use a positive base for arbitrary real exponents, or an appropriate integer-exponent domain.
A negative base with fractional exponents requires separate checking.
major_error_concepts: Since every expression is real-defined, ((-1)^2)^(1/2)=(-1)^1=-1.

cards.prompt: What is Zero and Negative Exponents? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: For nonzero a, a^0 = 1 and a^(-n) = 1/a^n. Negative exponents indicate reciprocals, not negative values; zero raised to a negative exponent is undefined.
required_concepts: Zero power of nonzero base is one.
major_error_concepts: Treating a^(-n) as -a^n.

cards.prompt: What is Rational Exponents? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Write m/n in lowest terms with n>0. For positive a, a^(m/n)=(nth-root(a))^m. For negative a this real convention is available when n is odd; an even reduced denominator has no real value. A zero base requires a positive exponent, while a negative exponent requires a nonzero base.
required_concepts: Reduce m/n with positive denominator before testing parity.
For a negative real base, the reduced denominator must be odd.
Negative exponents exclude a zero base.
accepted_variants: Reduce 2/6 to 1/3 first: (-8)^(2/6)=-2. In general negative bases allow an odd reduced root index, and negative powers exclude zero.
major_error_concepts: The real expression (-8)^(2/6) is undefined because the denominator 6 is even.

cards.prompt: What is Radical Expressions? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A radical represents a root. The principal square root is nonnegative, so sqrt(x squared) = |x| for real x; root products and quotients must respect real-domain conditions.
accepted_variants: Root notation with a specified index and radicand.
major_error_concepts: Simplifying sqrt(x squared) to x for unrestricted real x.

cards.prompt: What is Scientific Notation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Scientific notation writes a nonzero number as a times 10^n, with integer n and 1 <= |a| < 10. It separates a signed significant coefficient from the decimal scale.
required_concepts: Coefficient magnitude between one inclusive and ten exclusive.
major_error_concepts: Calling 45 times 10^3 normalized scientific notation.

cards.prompt: What is Algebraic Expression? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: An algebraic expression combines numbers, variables, and operations without asserting an equality. Evaluating it requires substituting allowed variable values and following the order of operations.
required_concepts: Combination of symbols and operations, not necessarily an equation.
Evaluation respects operation order and domain.
major_error_concepts: Solving an expression as if it asserted an equation.

cards.prompt: What is Polynomial? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A polynomial in x is a finite sum of coefficients times nonnegative integer powers of x. Negative or fractional powers of x and division by a variable do not appear in a polynomial expression.
required_concepts: Finite sum of nonnegative integer powers.
accepted_variants: A finite linear combination of monomials.
major_error_concepts: Calling 1/x or sqrt(x) a polynomial in x.

cards.prompt: What is Like Terms? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Like terms have the same variable factors with the same exponents and can be combined by adding coefficients. Different powers or different variable products are not like terms.
accepted_variants: Terms sharing the same monomial factor.
major_error_concepts: Combining x and x squared into one coefficient times x.

cards.prompt: What is Distributive Property? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: The distributive property is a(b+c)=ab+ac, with an analogous subtraction rule. It justifies expanding products over sums and reversing that expansion through factoring.
accepted_variants: Expansion of a product across summed terms.
major_error_concepts: Assuming exponents distribute across a sum, as in (a+b)^2=a^2+b^2.

cards.prompt: What is Factoring? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Factoring rewrites an expression as a product of factors without changing its value on its domain. Expanding the product reverses the process.
accepted_variants: Reverse distribution or decomposition into multiplicative parts.
major_error_concepts: Changing a sum into a product without preserving equality.

cards.prompt: What is Greatest Common Factor? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A greatest common factor is the largest shared integer coefficient factor together with the lowest shared powers of variable factors in the terms. Factoring it out leaves a product with a residual sum.
required_concepts: Shared factors use minimum common variable exponents.
accepted_variants: The maximal common monomial factor of the terms.
major_error_concepts: Taking the highest power present in any term rather than the power common to all.

cards.prompt: What is Difference of Squares? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A difference of squares factors as a squared minus b squared = (a-b)(a+b). The analogous real identity does not factor a sum of squares into the same binomials.
required_concepts: Conjugate-binomial factorization of a difference of squares.
major_error_concepts: Applying the formula unchanged to a squared plus b squared.

cards.prompt: What is Perfect-Square Trinomial? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A perfect-square trinomial has form a squared plus or minus 2ab plus b squared and factors as (a plus or minus b) squared. The middle term must match twice the product.
required_concepts: Square terms and matching signed middle term 2ab.
accepted_variants: The expanded square of a binomial.
major_error_concepts: Ignoring the middle term when recognizing a binomial square.

cards.prompt: What is Sum and Difference of Cubes? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A sum of cubes factors as a^3+b^3=(a+b)(a^2-ab+b^2); a difference factors as a^3-b^3=(a-b)(a^2+ab+b^2). The quadratic factor's middle sign is opposite the binomial's sign.
required_concepts: Correct sum and difference cube identities.
major_error_concepts: Using the difference-of-squares factors for cubes.

cards.prompt: What is Rational Expression? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A rational expression is a quotient of polynomials with a nonzero denominator. Simplifying common factors does not restore inputs excluded by the original denominator.
major_error_concepts: Cancelling common terms across addition or admitting an originally forbidden input.

cards.prompt: What is Expression Domain? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: The real domain of an expression is the set of inputs for which it is defined. Typical restrictions exclude zero denominators, negative even-root radicands, and nonpositive real logarithm arguments.
required_concepts: All inputs making the expression meaningful over the stated number system.
major_error_concepts: Assuming simplifying a formula automatically removes its original domain restrictions.

cards.prompt: What is Equation and Solution Set? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: An equation asserts equality of two expressions. A solution is an allowed value or tuple making that assertion true; the solution set can be empty, finite, or infinite.
required_concepts: Solutions satisfy it within the domain.
accepted_variants: A condition requiring two expressions to have the same value.
major_error_concepts: Calling every value substituted into an equation a solution.

cards.prompt: What is Equivalent Equations? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Equivalent equations have the same solution set on the stated domain. Adding equal quantities to both sides is reversible, whereas multiplying by an expression that can vanish may introduce or conceal exceptional cases.
required_concepts: Same solutions on the specified domain.
accepted_variants: Equations preserving exactly the same admissible solutions.
major_error_concepts: Assuming every algebraic transformation preserves equivalence automatically.

cards.prompt: What is Extraneous Solution? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: An extraneous solution satisfies a transformed equation but not the original one. Squaring, clearing restricted denominators, or changing branches can create candidates that must be checked against the original conditions.
required_concepts: Candidate fails the original equation or domain.
accepted_variants: A spurious solution introduced during algebraic manipulation.
major_error_concepts: Accepting every root of a squared equation without checking the unsquared relation.

cards.prompt: What is Linear Equation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A one-variable linear equation has form ax+b=0 with a nonzero and solution x=-b/a. If a is zero, the equation instead has either no solutions or all allowed values depending on b.
required_concepts: First-degree form and its nonzero-coefficient solution.
accepted_variants: An equation with the variable entering to the first power.
major_error_concepts: Dividing by a without considering whether it is zero.

cards.prompt: What is Linear Inequality? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A linear inequality compares affine expressions rather than requiring equality. Solving it uses order-preserving operations and reverses the comparison when multiplying or dividing by a negative number.
major_error_concepts: Using equation rules without the negative-scaling reversal.

cards.prompt: What is Compound Inequality? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Compound inequalities combine conditions using and or or. An and statement takes the intersection of solution sets, while an or statement takes their union.
required_concepts: And means intersection; or means union.
major_error_concepts: Using a union for simultaneous and conditions.

cards.prompt: What is Absolute-Value Equation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: For c nonnegative, |u|=c is equivalent to u=c or u=-c. If c is negative there is no real solution, because an absolute value cannot be negative.
required_concepts: Two signed cases for nonnegative c.
major_error_concepts: Solving only u=c and missing the negative branch when c is positive.

cards.prompt: What is Absolute-Value Inequality? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: For c positive, |u|<c means -c<u<c, while |u|>c means u<-c or u>c. Non-strict comparisons include the corresponding endpoints, and nonpositive thresholds need separate interpretation.
required_concepts: Less-than gives an interval; greater-than gives two outer regions.
major_error_concepts: Using an and condition for both outer branches of |u|>c.

cards.prompt: What is Proportion? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A proportion equates two ratios, a/b=c/d with nonzero denominators. It is equivalent to ad=bc on that domain; denominator restrictions remain essential.
required_concepts: Cross products agree when denominators are nonzero.
major_error_concepts: Cross-multiplying and retaining a solution that makes an original denominator zero.

cards.prompt: What is Quadratic Equation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A quadratic equation has form ax squared+bx+c=0 with a nonzero. Its solutions can be described by factoring, completing the square, or the quadratic formula, with real or complex roots depending on the discriminant.
required_concepts: Second-degree equation with nonzero leading coefficient.
major_error_concepts: Calling a linear equation quadratic after its quadratic coefficient vanishes.

cards.prompt: What is Zero-Product Property? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: The zero-product property says a product of real or complex numbers is zero exactly when at least one factor is zero. It applies after an equation is written as a product equal to zero, not to an arbitrary nonzero right side.
required_concepts: Product equals zero implies a zero factor.
accepted_variants: The no-zero-divisors rule for real or complex scalars.
major_error_concepts: Setting each factor to zero when their product equals five.

cards.prompt: What is Completing the Square? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Completing the square rewrites x squared+bx as (x+b/2) squared minus (b/2) squared. It converts quadratics into vertex form and leads to the quadratic formula while preserving equality.
required_concepts: Add and subtract the square of half the linear coefficient.
accepted_variants: Rewriting a quadratic around a perfect square.
major_error_concepts: Adding a term on one side of an equation without balancing it.

cards.prompt: What is Quadratic Formula? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: For ax squared+bx+c=0 with a nonzero, the roots are x=(-b plus or minus sqrt(b squared-4ac))/(2a). Both branches and the denominator enclosing the entire numerator are essential.
required_concepts: Correct formula including both signs and denominator 2a.
major_error_concepts: Dividing only the square-root term by 2a.

cards.prompt: What is Quadratic Discriminant? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: The quadratic discriminant is D=b squared-4ac. For real coefficients, positive D gives two distinct real roots, zero D a repeated real root, and negative D a nonreal conjugate pair.
required_concepts: Discriminant expression and the three root classifications.
accepted_variants: The quantity under the quadratic formula's square root.
major_error_concepts: Saying negative discriminant means no complex roots.

cards.prompt: What is Complex Number? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A complex number has form a+bi with real a and b and i squared=-1. Real numbers are included when b=0; the real and imaginary parts are a and b, respectively.
required_concepts: Real and imaginary components with i squared=-1.
accepted_variants: A number in the real-imaginary plane.
major_error_concepts: Calling the imaginary part bi rather than its real coefficient b under the standard convention.

cards.prompt: What is Complex Arithmetic? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Complex arithmetic adds real and imaginary parts separately and multiplies using distribution with i squared=-1. Division by a nonzero complex number can be performed using its conjugate.
major_error_concepts: Treating i squared as positive one.

cards.prompt: What is Complex Conjugate? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: The conjugate of a+bi is a-bi. Their product is a squared+b squared, the squared modulus; this makes conjugation useful for rationalizing complex denominators.
required_concepts: Product with conjugate is the squared modulus.
major_error_concepts: Negating both the real and imaginary parts when taking a conjugate.

cards.prompt: What is Linear System? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A linear system consists of linear equations required to hold simultaneously. Its solution is a tuple satisfying every equation, geometrically an intersection of lines, planes, or higher-dimensional affine sets.
accepted_variants: A set of coupled linear constraints.
major_error_concepts: Accepting a tuple that satisfies only one equation.

cards.prompt: What is Substitution Method? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Substitution solves a system by expressing one variable from an equation and replacing it in the others. The resulting conditions must still retain any domain or division restrictions from the substitution.
required_concepts: Replace a variable by an equivalent expression from another equation.
major_error_concepts: Dividing by a potentially zero expression without treating its exceptional case.

cards.prompt: What is Elimination Method? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Elimination combines equations so a variable cancels, typically after multiplying equations by suitable nonzero constants. Reversible row-style operations preserve the simultaneous solution set.
accepted_variants: Addition method for simultaneous linear equations.
major_error_concepts: Dropping an equation after a nonreversible manipulation and claiming full equivalence.

cards.prompt: What is Linear-System Solution Types? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A linear system is consistent if it has at least one solution and inconsistent otherwise. A consistent system may have a unique solution or infinitely many, depending on independent constraints and free variables.
required_concepts: Distinguish unique and infinitely many solutions.
accepted_variants: The existence and multiplicity classification of linear systems.
major_error_concepts: Assuming any system with as many equations as variables has exactly one solution.

cards.prompt: What is Augmented Matrix? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: An augmented matrix records a linear system's coefficients together with its right-hand-side column. Columns correspond to a fixed variable order and rows to equations.
accepted_variants: A matrix encoding of the system.
major_error_concepts: Reordering only one row's variables while keeping the matrix column interpretation unchanged.

cards.prompt: What is Elementary Row Operations? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Elementary row operations swap rows, multiply a row by a nonzero scalar, or add a multiple of one row to another. These operations preserve the solution set of an augmented linear system.
required_concepts: Row scaling factor must be nonzero.
major_error_concepts: Multiplying a row by zero and claiming equivalence.

cards.prompt: What is Two-by-Two Determinant? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: The determinant of the two-by-two matrix with rows (a,b) and (c,d) is ad-bc. A nonzero determinant means the corresponding square linear system has a unique solution for every right-hand side.
required_concepts: Nonzero determinant characterizes invertibility in this case.
major_error_concepts: Using ad+bc as the determinant.

cards.prompt: What is Nonlinear System? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A nonlinear system contains at least one equation nonlinear in the unknowns. Its solutions are simultaneous intersections; substitution or elimination can produce multiple isolated solutions or require domain checks.
major_error_concepts: Assuming the linear system trichotomy limits a nonlinear system to one or infinitely many solutions.

cards.prompt: What is Function? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A function assigns exactly one output to each input in its domain. Different inputs may share an output, but one allowed input cannot have two distinct outputs under the same function rule.
required_concepts: Exactly one output per allowed input.
major_error_concepts: Requiring every output to have exactly one input as part of the basic function definition.

cards.prompt: What is Domain and Range? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A function's domain is its allowed input set; its range is the set of outputs actually attained. The codomain, when specified, may contain values outside the range.
major_error_concepts: Swapping domain and range.

cards.prompt: What is Function Notation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Function notation f(x) denotes the output of f at input x, not multiplication of f by x. Evaluating f(a+h) requires substituting the entire expression a+h wherever the input variable appears.
accepted_variants: The value of a function at a specified argument.
major_error_concepts: Assuming f(a+h)=f(a)+f(h) for every function.

cards.prompt: What is Function Graph? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: The graph of y=f(x) is the set of ordered pairs (x,f(x)) for allowed inputs x. It displays the relation between input and output, including domain gaps and multiple inputs sharing an output.
required_concepts: All input-output ordered pairs on the domain.
accepted_variants: A coordinate representation of a function.
major_error_concepts: Drawing a continuous connection across an excluded domain point without noting the gap.

cards.prompt: What is Vertical-Line Test? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A graph in the xy-plane represents y as a function of x exactly when each vertical line meets it in at most one point. This tests uniqueness of output for each input.
required_concepts: At most one graph point for each fixed x.
major_error_concepts: Using horizontal lines as the general function test.

cards.prompt: What is Intercepts? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: An x-intercept is a point (x,0) on the graph; for y=f(x), x must be in the domain and satisfy f(x)=0. A y-intercept is a point (0,y) on the graph; for a function it exists exactly when 0 is in the domain, and then it is (0,f(0)).
required_concepts: An x-intercept is a graph point with output zero.
A y-intercept is a graph point with input zero; a function needs zero in its domain.
major_error_concepts: A y-intercept exists only if the output y is in the function's input domain.

cards.prompt: What is Slope? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: The slope of a nonvertical line is change in y divided by change in x between distinct points. A vertical line has undefined slope, while a horizontal line has slope zero.
required_concepts: Rise divided by run with nonzero horizontal change.
accepted_variants: Constant rate of change along a line.
major_error_concepts: Assigning zero slope to a vertical line.

cards.prompt: What is Line Equations? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A nonvertical line can be written y=mx+b or y-y1=m(x-x1). Slope m describes its rate of change, while b is its y-intercept; vertical lines have form x=c.
accepted_variants: Equivalent coordinate equations for a straight line.
major_error_concepts: Forcing every vertical line into y=mx+b with finite m.

cards.prompt: What is Average Rate of Change? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: The average rate of change of f from a to b is (f(b)-f(a))/(b-a) for a not equal to b. It is the slope of the secant line through the corresponding graph points.
major_error_concepts: Using f(b)/b while ignoring the first endpoint.

cards.prompt: What is Increasing and Decreasing Functions? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A function is increasing on an interval if larger inputs give larger outputs, and decreasing if larger inputs give smaller outputs, under the strict convention. Nondecreasing and nonincreasing allow equality.
required_concepts: Compare outputs for ordered inputs throughout the interval.
accepted_variants: Directional change of function values across an interval.
major_error_concepts: Inferring global increase from two selected endpoints alone.

cards.prompt: What is Function Extrema? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A local maximum or minimum compares a function value with nearby domain values; an absolute extremum compares it with every domain value. A function can have local extrema without attaining an absolute maximum or minimum.
accepted_variants: Local or global high and low values.
major_error_concepts: Calling every local maximum the absolute maximum.

cards.prompt: What is Even and Odd Functions? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: On a domain symmetric about zero, an even function satisfies f(-x)=f(x) and an odd function satisfies f(-x)=-f(x). These correspond to y-axis and origin symmetry, respectively.
accepted_variants: Reflection or origin symmetry of function values.
major_error_concepts: Classifying every function as either even or odd.

cards.prompt: What is Piecewise Function? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A piecewise-defined function uses different formulas on specified parts of its domain. Endpoint inclusion and overlap rules must still assign exactly one value to each allowed input.
required_concepts: Formula selected by the input region.
Endpoint and overlap definitions must be consistent.
major_error_concepts: Applying every branch simultaneously to an input regardless of its conditions.

cards.prompt: What is Graph Transformations? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: In g(x)=a f(b(x-h))+k, h and k shift the graph horizontally and vertically; a changes vertical scale and possibly reflects, while nonzero b changes horizontal scale inversely and may reflect. Domain changes follow the transformed input.
required_concepts: Input transformations act horizontally and output transformations vertically.
accepted_variants: Translations, scalings, and reflections of a parent function.
major_error_concepts: Claiming f(x-h) shifts left when h is positive.

cards.prompt: What is Function Arithmetic? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Function sums, products, and quotients act pointwise on inputs where all components are defined. A quotient additionally excludes inputs making its denominator function zero.
major_error_concepts: Adding domains by union when both functions must be evaluated at the same input.

cards.prompt: What is Function Composition? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: The composition (f composed with g)(x)=f(g(x)) applies g first and f second. Its domain includes only inputs in g's domain whose outputs lie in f's domain.
required_concepts: Output of inner must be allowed input of outer.
major_error_concepts: Assuming composition is commutative.

cards.prompt: What is One-to-One Function? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A function is one-to-one if distinct inputs always have distinct outputs. Equivalently f(a)=f(b) implies a=b; this is stronger than merely being a function.
required_concepts: No two distinct inputs share an output.
major_error_concepts: Confusing one output per input with one-to-one behavior.

cards.prompt: What is Inverse Function? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: An inverse function reverses a one-to-one function between its domain and range. It satisfies f^-1(f(x))=x on the original domain and exchanges domain and range; a noninjective function needs a suitable domain restriction first.
required_concepts: Reverse input-output correspondence for an injective function.
Inverse notation is not reciprocal notation.
accepted_variants: A function undoing another function on its image.
major_error_concepts: Interpreting f^-1(x) as 1/f(x).

cards.prompt: What is Horizontal-Line Test? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A function graph passes the horizontal-line test when every horizontal line meets it in at most one point. This means each output comes from at most one input and the function is one-to-one.
required_concepts: At most one input for a fixed output.
major_error_concepts: Using this test instead of the vertical-line test to determine whether a relation is a function at all.

cards.prompt: What is Polynomial Degree and End Behavior? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: For a nonzero polynomial, degree is its highest exponent with nonzero coefficient. The degree's parity and leading coefficient's sign determine the end behavior as x tends toward positive or negative infinity.
required_concepts: Leading term determines far-left and far-right behavior.
major_error_concepts: Using a low-order term to determine eventual end behavior.

cards.prompt: What is Zero Multiplicity? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A zero r of multiplicity m contributes a factor (x-r)^m. A real polynomial typically crosses the axis at an odd-multiplicity zero and touches without changing sign at an even-multiplicity zero.
required_concepts: Multiplicity is the repeated factor exponent.
Odd/even multiplicity determines local sign change.
major_error_concepts: Claiming an even-multiplicity root always changes the polynomial's sign.

cards.prompt: What is Remainder Theorem? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: When a polynomial f(x) is divided by x-c, its constant remainder is f(c), because f(x)=(x-c)q(x)+r gives f(c)=r. The same evaluation works for a divisor a(x-c) with nonzero a; for ax-b the remainder is f(b/a).
required_concepts: The remainder on division by x-c is f(c).
The root of a general nonconstant linear divisor is the evaluation point.
accepted_variants: If f(x)=(2x-2)q(x)+r, substitute x=1 to get r=f(1); monicity is unnecessary.
major_error_concepts: When dividing by 2x-2, the remainder cannot be obtained by evaluating f(1).

cards.prompt: What is Factor Theorem? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: The factor theorem says x-c is a factor of polynomial f exactly when f(c)=0. It connects polynomial roots to linear factors.
required_concepts: Zero evaluation if and only if the linear factor divides the polynomial.
major_error_concepts: Inferring x-c is a factor when f(c) is merely small but nonzero.

cards.prompt: What is Synthetic Division? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Synthetic division is a compact coefficient algorithm for dividing a polynomial by a monic linear factor x-c. Missing powers must be represented by zero coefficients to preserve positions.
required_concepts: Coefficient shortcut for division by x-c.
Include zero coefficients for absent powers.
major_error_concepts: Dropping missing-degree placeholders and interpreting the resulting coefficients unchanged.

cards.prompt: What is Rational-Zero Theorem? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: For an integer-coefficient polynomial, any rational zero in lowest terms p/q has p dividing the constant coefficient and q dividing the leading coefficient. The theorem supplies candidates, not a guarantee that each candidate is a zero.
required_concepts: Numerator divides constant and denominator divides leading coefficient.
major_error_concepts: Claiming every listed rational candidate is an actual root.

cards.prompt: What is Fundamental Theorem of Algebra? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Every nonconstant polynomial with complex coefficients has a complex root and factors completely into linear factors over the complex numbers. A degree-n polynomial has n complex roots counting multiplicity.
required_concepts: Complex roots exist and factorization is complete over complex numbers.
major_error_concepts: Claiming a degree-n polynomial necessarily has n distinct real roots.

cards.prompt: What is Polynomial Inequality? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A polynomial inequality is solved by determining the polynomial's sign on intervals separated by real zeros. Include or exclude zeros according to whether the comparison is non-strict or strict.
required_concepts: Zeros partition the line into constant-sign intervals.
major_error_concepts: Assuming the sign flips at every root regardless of multiplicity.

cards.prompt: What is Vertical Asymptote? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A vertical asymptote of a rational function occurs where the function becomes unbounded as the input approaches a finite value from at least one side. After common factors are cancelled, remaining real denominator zeros give the usual candidates.
required_concepts: Unbounded approach near a finite input.
Check cancellation before identifying denominator-zero asymptotes.
accepted_variants: A vertical line approached with divergent function values.
major_error_concepts: Calling every original denominator zero a vertical asymptote even after complete cancellation.

cards.prompt: What is Horizontal Asymptote? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A horizontal asymptote is y=L when f(x) approaches L as x tends to positive or negative infinity. For rational functions, degree comparison gives zero when numerator degree is lower and the leading-coefficient ratio when degrees match.
required_concepts: Finite limiting height at an infinite tail.
accepted_variants: A limiting horizontal line at large input magnitude.
major_error_concepts: Claiming a graph can never cross a horizontal asymptote.

cards.prompt: What is Slant Asymptote? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A slant asymptote is a nonhorizontal line whose vertical difference from the graph tends to zero at infinity. For a rational function with numerator degree one higher than denominator degree, polynomial division gives the line.
required_concepts: Difference from a line tends to zero.
One-degree gap gives the usual rational-function case.
major_error_concepts: Using the quotient line as the exact function while omitting a nonzero remainder.

cards.prompt: What is Removable Hole? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A removable hole is an excluded input at which a simplified function has a finite limiting value. Cancelling a common factor can reveal the hole's height but does not make the original function defined there.
required_concepts: Original domain exclusion with finite simplified approach.
Distinguish the original function from its extension.
accepted_variants: A removable discontinuity caused by a cancelled denominator factor.
major_error_concepts: Filling the hole automatically after cancellation without redefining the function.

cards.prompt: What is Rational Inequality? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A rational inequality is solved by a sign chart using numerator zeros and excluded denominator zeros. Multiplying by an expression of unknown sign requires case distinctions rather than preserving the inequality blindly.
required_concepts: Partition by zeros and undefined points.
Respect sign changes and denominator exclusions.
major_error_concepts: Multiplying through by an unknown-sign denominator without reversing or splitting cases.

cards.prompt: What is Power Function? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A power function has form f(x)=a x^p for fixed constants a and p on a specified domain. Its parity, real domain, and shape depend on the exponent, especially for negative or noninteger powers.
accepted_variants: A monomial-type function with a general exponent.
major_error_concepts: Confusing a^x with a power function of x under this definition.

cards.prompt: What is Exponential Function? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: An exponential function has form f(x)=b^x with b positive and b not equal to one. It has positive outputs, is increasing for b>1, and decreasing for 0<b<1.
required_concepts: Fixed positive base and variable exponent.
Growth versus decay by base range.
accepted_variants: A constant-ratio function over equal input increments.
major_error_concepts: Allowing an arbitrary negative base as a real-valued exponential on all real inputs.

cards.prompt: What is Exponential Growth and Decay? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: An exponential model y=Ae^(kt) has constant proportional change over equal time intervals. Positive k gives growth and negative k decay; this is a modeling assumption rather than a universal property of real populations or quantities.
required_concepts: Sign of k determines direction for positive A.
major_error_concepts: Confusing equal percentage change with equal absolute change.

cards.prompt: What is Compound-Growth Formula? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: The compound-interest formula A=P(1+r/n)^(nt) describes a fixed nominal annual rate r compounded n times yearly with no additional cash flows. Continuous compounding uses A=Pe^(rt); the formula is a mathematical model, not a promised real-world return.
required_concepts: Identify principal, rate, compounding frequency, and time.
Assume the stated rate and no extra deposits or withdrawals.
major_error_concepts: Treating a quoted model rate as a guaranteed investment outcome.

cards.prompt: What is Logarithm? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: The logarithm log_b(x) is the exponent y satisfying b^y=x, for b positive, b not equal to one, and x positive. It is the inverse of an exponential function on its range.
major_error_concepts: Allowing zero or negative arguments in an ordinary real logarithm.

cards.prompt: What is Logarithm Properties? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: For positive u and v and a valid base, log_b(uv)=log_b u+log_b v and log_b(u/v)=log_b u-log_b v. The power rule log_b(u^r)=r log_b u assumes a domain where the expressions are valid.
required_concepts: Products become sums and quotients differences.
accepted_variants: Logarithmic product, quotient, and power identities.
major_error_concepts: Using log(u+v)=log u+log v.

cards.prompt: What is Change of Base? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: The change-of-base formula is log_b x=log_a x/log_a b for positive valid bases a and b and positive x. The denominator is nonzero because b is not one.
required_concepts: Log of the argument divided by log of the old base.
accepted_variants: Conversion of a logarithm to another base.
major_error_concepts: Reversing numerator and denominator.

cards.prompt: What is Logarithmic Equation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A logarithmic equation can be converted using inverse exponential relations or valid log identities, while retaining positive-argument restrictions. Candidate solutions outside the original logarithm domain are rejected.
required_concepts: Use inverse relations while preserving argument positivity.
accepted_variants: An equation involving logarithms with explicit domain checks.
major_error_concepts: Accepting a root that makes an original log argument negative after combining logs.

cards.prompt: What is Exponential–Logarithm Inverses? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Exponential and logarithmic functions with the same base undo one another: log_b(b^x)=x and b^(log_b x)=x for x positive in the second identity. Their graphs are reflections across y=x.
required_concepts: Two inverse identities with domain restriction.
major_error_concepts: Applying b^(log_b x)=x to nonpositive real x.

cards.prompt: What is Radian Measure? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A radian is the angle subtending an arc equal in length to the circle's radius. The relation is theta=s/r, and one full revolution is 2 pi radians or 360 degrees.
accepted_variants: Natural angular measure from circular arc length.
major_error_concepts: Equating pi radians with 360 degrees.

cards.prompt: What is Unit Circle? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: The unit circle has radius one and center at the origin. The point reached by angle theta in standard position is (cos theta,sin theta), linking trigonometric values to coordinates.
accepted_variants: The coordinate circle defining trigonometric functions.
major_error_concepts: Swapping the sine and cosine coordinates.

cards.prompt: What is Sine? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Sine of an angle is the y-coordinate of its unit-circle point. For an acute right-triangle angle it is opposite side divided by hypotenuse, and its values lie between -1 and 1.
major_error_concepts: Using adjacent over hypotenuse as sine.

cards.prompt: What is Cosine? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Cosine of an angle is the x-coordinate of its unit-circle point. For an acute right-triangle angle it is adjacent side divided by hypotenuse, and its values lie between -1 and 1.
major_error_concepts: Using opposite over hypotenuse as cosine.

cards.prompt: What is Tangent? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Tangent is tan theta=sin theta/cos theta where cosine is nonzero. For acute right-triangle angles it is opposite over adjacent, and its period is pi radians.
accepted_variants: The ratio of vertical to horizontal unit-circle coordinates.
major_error_concepts: Defining tangent at pi/2 by ordinary real division.

cards.prompt: What is Reciprocal Trigonometric Functions? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Secant, cosecant, and cotangent are reciprocal trigonometric functions: sec=1/cos, csc=1/sin, and cot=cos/sin where denominators are nonzero. Reciprocals differ from inverse-angle functions.
required_concepts: Correct reciprocal definitions and nonzero denominators.
major_error_concepts: Equating cosecant with arcsine.

cards.prompt: What is Pythagorean Identities? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: The identity sin squared theta+cos squared theta=1 follows from the unit circle. Dividing on valid domains gives 1+tan squared theta=sec squared theta and 1+cot squared theta=csc squared theta.
major_error_concepts: Using sin theta+cos theta=1 as a universal identity.

cards.prompt: What is Special-Angle Values? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: The special angles pi/6, pi/4, and pi/3 have exact sine-cosine pairs (1/2,sqrt(3)/2), (sqrt(2)/2,sqrt(2)/2), and (sqrt(3)/2,1/2). These follow from 30-60-90 and 45-45-90 triangle ratios.
required_concepts: Correct exact values and angle correspondence.
major_error_concepts: Interchanging the pi/6 and pi/3 sine values.

cards.prompt: What is Reference Angle? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A reference angle is the acute angle between an angle's terminal side and the x-axis. Trigonometric magnitudes follow the reference angle, while signs follow the quadrant; quadrantal angles are handled directly.
major_error_concepts: Assigning all trigonometric functions the reference angle's positive sign in every quadrant.

cards.prompt: What is Sinusoidal Graph? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A sinusoid y=A sin(B(x-h))+D has amplitude |A|, period 2 pi/|B| for B nonzero, horizontal shift h, and midline y=D. Cosine has the same parameter interpretation.
required_concepts: Amplitude absolute A and inverse-|B| period.
accepted_variants: The parameterized sine or cosine graph.
major_error_concepts: Using 2 pi times |B| as the period.

cards.prompt: What is Phase Shift? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Phase shift is the horizontal displacement of a periodic graph relative to its chosen reference form. For sin(Bx-C), factoring the argument shows shift C/B when B is nonzero.
required_concepts: Factor the input coefficient before reading horizontal shift.
major_error_concepts: Reading C alone as the shift in sin(Bx-C) for arbitrary B.

cards.prompt: What is Inverse Trigonometric Functions? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Inverse trigonometric functions return principal angles after restricting the original function's domain. Standard ranges are [-pi/2,pi/2] for arcsine, [0,pi] for arccosine, and (-pi/2,pi/2) for arctangent.
required_concepts: Principal-angle branch from an injective restriction.
major_error_concepts: Interpreting sin^-1 x as the reciprocal of sine in inverse-function notation.

cards.prompt: What is Angle-Sum Identities? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Angle-sum formulas express sine and cosine of combined angles: sin(a+b)=sin a cos b+cos a sin b and cos(a+b)=cos a cos b-sin a sin b. Difference identities follow by replacing b with -b.
required_concepts: Correct sum formulas and cosine minus sign.
major_error_concepts: Assuming sin(a+b)=sin a+sin b.

cards.prompt: What is Double-Angle Identities? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Double-angle identities include sin(2x)=2 sin x cos x and cos(2x)=cos squared x-sin squared x=2 cos squared x-1=1-2 sin squared x. They are special cases of angle addition.
required_concepts: Correct sine and cosine double-angle identities.
accepted_variants: Trigonometric identities for twice an angle.
major_error_concepts: Equating sin(2x) with 2 sin x for every x.

cards.prompt: What is Half-Angle Identities? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Half-angle identities give sin squared(x/2)=(1-cos x)/2 and cos squared(x/2)=(1+cos x)/2. Taking square roots requires choosing signs from the quadrant of the half-angle.
accepted_variants: Half-angle magnitude identities with sign selection.
major_error_concepts: Always choosing the positive root for a half-angle sine or cosine.

cards.prompt: What is Trigonometric Equation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A trigonometric equation seeks angles satisfying the original relation on the stated domain. Inverse functions give principal candidates, while symmetry and periodicity generate other solutions; transformations can introduce extraneous values or lose branches.
required_concepts: Principal values are not always the full solution set.
accepted_variants: Solving an angle condition with branch and period bookkeeping.
major_error_concepts: Reporting only arcsin(c) as every solution of sin x=c.

cards.prompt: What is Law of Sines? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: The law of sines states a/sin A=b/sin B=c/sin C for opposite sides and angles of a triangle. In side-side-angle data, more than one triangle or no triangle may fit, so the ambiguous case requires care.
required_concepts: Pair each side with its opposite angle.
major_error_concepts: Pairing a side with an adjacent angle or assuming SSA always gives one triangle.

cards.prompt: What is Law of Cosines? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: The law of cosines states c squared=a squared+b squared-2ab cos C, where C is the included angle opposite c. It reduces to the Pythagorean theorem for a right included angle.
required_concepts: Included-angle relation with minus 2ab cos C.
accepted_variants: Cosine rule for a general triangle.
major_error_concepts: Using an angle not between a and b in the displayed formula.

cards.term: Triangle Area from Two Sides and an Angle
cards.prompt: What is Triangle Area from Two Sides and an Angle? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: The area of a triangle with two sides a and b and their included angle C is one-half ab sin C. The angle must be the one between the selected sides.
required_concepts: Half the product of two sides times sine of their included angle.
major_error_concepts: Using cosine instead of sine in the included-angle area formula.

cards.prompt: What is Plane Vector? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A plane vector has magnitude and direction and can be represented by components (v_x,v_y). Vectors add componentwise, scalar multiplication rescales them, and magnitude is sqrt(v_x squared+v_y squared).
required_concepts: Component representation with magnitude and direction.
major_error_concepts: Adding magnitudes alone to determine the magnitude of a general vector sum.

cards.prompt: What is Dot Product? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: The dot product u dot v equals u_x v_x+u_y v_y and also |u||v|cos theta. It is a scalar; nonzero vectors are perpendicular exactly when their dot product is zero.
major_error_concepts: Treating the dot product as another vector.

cards.prompt: What is Parametric Equations? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Parametric equations describe coordinates as functions of a parameter, such as x=f(t), y=g(t). They can encode orientation and repeated traversal that may be lost when the parameter is eliminated.
required_concepts: Coordinates depend on a common parameter.
major_error_concepts: Assuming eliminating the parameter preserves direction and traversal count.

cards.prompt: What is Polar Coordinates? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Polar coordinates describe a point using radius r and angle theta, with x=r cos theta and y=r sin theta. Representations are not unique because angles repeat and negative radii reverse direction.
major_error_concepts: Assuming one point has exactly one polar coordinate pair.

cards.prompt: What is Complex Polar Form? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A nonzero complex number can be written z=r(cos theta+i sin theta), where r=|z| and theta is an argument defined modulo 2 pi. Multiplication multiplies moduli and adds arguments.
required_concepts: Arguments are not unique modulo full turns.
accepted_variants: Trigonometric or polar form of a complex number.
major_error_concepts: Adding moduli when multiplying complex numbers.

cards.prompt: What is De Moivre's Formula? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: De Moivre's formula gives [cos theta+i sin theta]^n=cos(n theta)+i sin(n theta) for integer n. Combined with modulus powers and all angle branches, it supports powers and roots of complex numbers.
required_concepts: Root finding must retain distinct branches.
major_error_concepts: Reporting only one root for every nonzero complex nth-root problem.

cards.prompt: What is Conic Section? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Conic sections are curves obtained by intersecting a plane with a double cone; nondegenerate types are ellipses, parabolas, and hyperbolas, with circles as special ellipses. Coordinate equations classify them through quadratic forms and parameters.
required_concepts: Plane-cone intersections and the nondegenerate families.
accepted_variants: Quadratic plane curves of conic type.
major_error_concepts: Claiming every conic must be a closed curve.

cards.prompt: What is Circle? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A circle is the set of points a fixed distance r from a center (h,k). Its equation is (x-h) squared+(y-k) squared=r squared with r positive for a nondegenerate circle.
major_error_concepts: Reading r squared itself as the radius.

cards.prompt: What is Parabola? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A parabola is the locus of points equally distant from a focus and a directrix. A vertical-axis form is (x-h) squared=4p(y-k), with vertex (h,k) and signed focal displacement p nonzero.
required_concepts: Equal distances to focus and directrix.
Vertex and signed p determine opening direction.
accepted_variants: The focus-directrix conic of eccentricity one.
major_error_concepts: Assuming every parabola opens upward.

cards.prompt: What is Ellipse? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: An ellipse is the locus whose sum of distances to two fixed foci is constant. A horizontal-major-axis form has (x-h) squared/a squared+(y-k) squared/b squared=1 with a>b>0 and focal relation c squared=a squared-b squared.
major_error_concepts: Using c squared=a squared+b squared for an ellipse.

cards.prompt: What is Hyperbola? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A hyperbola is the locus whose absolute difference of distances to two foci is a fixed positive constant. In (x-h) squared/a squared-(y-k) squared/b squared=1, its focal relation is c squared=a squared+b squared and it has two branches.
required_concepts: Two branches and plus-sign focal relation.
major_error_concepts: Using the ellipse's sum-of-distances definition for a hyperbola.

cards.prompt: What is Sequence? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A sequence is a function whose domain is an ordered set of integer indices, commonly the positive integers. An explicit formula gives a term directly, while a recursive definition gives it from earlier terms and starting values.
major_error_concepts: Giving a recurrence without the starting data needed to determine its terms.

cards.prompt: What is Arithmetic Sequence? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: An arithmetic sequence has constant difference d between consecutive terms. With first term a1, its nth term is a_n=a1+(n-1)d.
major_error_concepts: Using a_n=a1+nd when indexing the first term as n=1.

cards.prompt: What is Geometric Sequence? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A geometric sequence has constant ratio r between consecutive terms where that ratio description is defined. Its standard form is a_n=a1 r^(n-1), with behavior depending on the magnitude and sign of r.
major_error_concepts: Confusing a constant ratio with a constant difference.

cards.prompt: What is Summation Notation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Sigma notation sums an indexed expression over a specified finite or infinite index range. The index is a placeholder; limits determine which terms appear.
major_error_concepts: Ignoring the lower limit when counting or evaluating terms.

cards.prompt: What is Finite Progression Sums? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A finite arithmetic series has sum n(a1+a_n)/2. A finite geometric series with ratio r not equal to one has sum a1(1-r^n)/(1-r); for r=1 the sum is n a1.
required_concepts: Correct arithmetic and geometric finite-sum forms.
accepted_variants: Closed forms for sums of finite progressions.
major_error_concepts: Using the infinite geometric formula for a finite number of terms.

cards.prompt: What is Infinite Geometric Series? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: An infinite geometric series with first term a and ratio r converges to a/(1-r) when |r|<1. Outside that range it diverges unless the series is the trivial all-zero case.
major_error_concepts: Using the formula as a convergent sum for r=2.

cards.prompt: What is Binomial Theorem? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: For a nonnegative integer n, the binomial theorem expands (a+b)^n as the sum from k=0 to n of binomial(n,k) a^(n-k)b^k. The coefficients count choices and follow Pascal's triangle.
required_concepts: Finite formula assumes nonnegative integer n.
major_error_concepts: Omitting mixed terms and using only a^n+b^n.

cards.prompt: What is Induction Principle? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Mathematical induction proves a statement for all integers from a starting index by proving a base case and showing that truth at a general index implies truth at the next. Both parts are necessary.
required_concepts: The inductive assumption concerns an arbitrary valid index.
accepted_variants: A domino-style proof principle for indexed statements.
major_error_concepts: Checking several numerical cases and claiming an induction proof.

description: A definition-recall course deck covering core concepts in College Algebra and Precalculus.
